quote: If that sort of trick actually worked, then more regulations would correlate to higher economic growth as society moved from local to global optima. But when some person or interest group gets enough power to start doing everything they think is a good idea, history says that what actually happens is Revolutionary France or Soviet Russia.
content: The inference is a non sequitur and the history is a false dichotomy. That well-designed rules can improve outcomes does not predict that the count of regulations correlates with growth, since regulations vary in quality and the marginal one is not a random draw from the good ones; and the alternatives to laissez-faire are not exhausted by the Terror and the Soviet Union. The fastest sustained growth episodes on record, Japan, Korea and Taiwan after 1950 and China after 1980, were run by states that directed credit, protected industries and planned exports (Amsden, Asia’s Next Giant, 1989; Rodrik, One Economics, Many Recipes, 2007), and the institutional literature finds that state capacity and the rule of law, both of which are regulation, are among the strongest correlates of long-run growth. The essay’s “core argument for libertarianism” is also not the libertarians’: Hayek’s case is the knowledge argument (“The Use of Knowledge in Society,” American Economic Review, 1945), that prices aggregate dispersed information no planner can collect, which is a claim about information and not about distrust of lovely theories. The analogy to science may still be apt; the economics it is drawn from is a sketch.

quote: Instead, we try to harness the individual scientist’s stubborn desire to prove their personal theory, by saying: “Make a new experimental prediction, and do the experiment. If you’re right, and the experiment is replicated, you win.”
content: This account of science as a mechanism that turns individual bias into collective reliability is the standard one in the sociology and philosophy of science, and it has names: Merton’s norms and the priority rule (1942, 1957), Hull’s Science as a Process (1988), Kitcher’s division of cognitive labour (Kitcher (1990)), and Strevens’s analysis of why the priority rule makes stubborn scientists useful (Strevens (2003)). The essay presents it as its own observation. The specific clause on which the mechanism depends, “and the experiment is replicated,” was not, when the essay was written, operating: about one per cent of published psychology studies were replications (Makel, Plucker & Hegarty (2012)), and the systematic replication efforts that began a few years later found that the literature this book cites throughout, from priming to ego depletion, had been built without the check the essay says gives scientists “a motive to be honest.” The essay is right that the system degrades gracefully; the finding of the following decade was how far it had degraded while everyone assumed the clause was in force.

quote: Science first came to know itself as a rebellion against trusting the word of Aristotle.
content: Book I’s annotations on the Baconian origin story apply here. The seventeenth-century natural philosophers were mostly trained Aristotelians who kept much of Aristotle (Harvey, Galileo’s method of resolution and composition, the scholastic logic of the universities), the rebellion against “authority” was largely Bacon’s and Descartes’s rhetoric about their predecessors, and the institution that made experiment a public practice, the Royal Society, was founded on Boyle’s procedures for witnessing, that is, on a new way of trusting testimony rather than on not trusting anyone (Shapin and Schaffer, Leviathan and the Air-Pump, 1985). “Let us trust no one, not even ourselves” is a good slogan for a norm that emerged; it is not what the architects said, and the architects’ actual innovation, replacing the authority of texts with the authority of a community of witnesses, is the opposite of the individualist reading the essay gives it.
